Article Title: No stopping SKY! Suryakumar Yadav sends big message with 60 off 21 balls in Syed Mushtaq
Article Text:
Mumbai’s Suryakumar Yadav

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former India T20I captain Suryakumar Yadav began his Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy 2026-27 campaign with an unbeaten 60 off just 21 balls as Mumbai defeated Hyderabad by seven wickets in their Elite Group D match on Saturday (November 14) at Jadavpur University Campus 2nd Ground in Kolkata.Chasing a target of 173, Suryakumar came in at No. 4 and struck six fours and five sixes to help Mumbai complete the chase in 13.1 overs. He reached his half-century in just 15 balls and shared a 65-run partnership off 23 balls with Musheer Khan for the third wicket.Musheer, younger brother of Sarfaraz Khan, also scored a half-century in Mumbai's opening match of the tournament. He made 51 off 24 balls, hitting six fours and three sixes, before being dismissed by Ajay Dev Goud in the 12th over.Earlier, Musheer had also shared a 49-run stand off 26 balls with wicketkeeper Hardik Tamore for the second wicket. Musheer contributed 41 runs off 18 balls during that partnership.Shivam Dube, who has won two T20 World Cups with India, finished the chase with a six off the first ball of the 14th over, bowled by Hyderabad captain Chama V Milind. He remained unbeaten on 13 off five balls while batting at No. 5.Earlier, Mumbai restricted Hyderabad to 172 in 20 overs. Maxwell Swaminathan picked up three wickets for 23 runs in his four overs, while Dube and Sairaj Patil took two wickets each.For Hyderabad, Abhirath Reddy top-scored with 35 off 24 balls, while Kodimela Himateja contributed 25 off 16 balls.After starting their campaign with a seven-wicket win, Mumbai will face Gujarat in their next match on Monday (November 16) at the same venue. They will then take on Goa, Vidarbha, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Uttarakhand on November 18, 20, 22, 24 and 26, respectively.
Article Summary: Mumbai beat Hyderabad by seven wickets in Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy 2026-27. Former India captain Suryakumar Yadav scored 60 off just 21 balls. Shivam Dube finished the chase with a six off the first ball of the 14th over.

Article Title: 'Are we in kindergarten?': Ex-India spinner backs Khawaja, tears into Cummins' sandpapergate explanation
Article Text:
Usman Khawaja, Pat Cummins

Warner accuses Cricket Australia of cover-up

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former India spinner Murali Kartik has backed Usman Khawaja in the ongoing debate over the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, questioning Pat Cummins ' claim that he was unaware of the plan to use sandpaper during the Cape Town Test against South Africa.The controversy resurfaced after Khawaja made several claims in his memoir, Sabr, suggesting that the entire Australian team, including current Test captain Cummins, knew about the plan to alter the condition of the ball.Cummins rejected the allegations during a press conference on Friday, describing Khawaja's claims as "complete and utter nonsense".Kartik, however, sided with Khawaja and said it was difficult to believe that the bowlers were unaware of a plan that was allegedly being carried out for their benefit."When it happened, there was a mini probe and three players were sent to the galley. Everyone knew what was happening. The problem is that if and when something like this happens, it's for the sake of the bowlers. 'Devious, underhand, wrong' - let's not go there. Once that is happening, and if I am the bowler while the other two guys are doing it for me, I don't know how anyone can say that I didn't know about it. How can anyone say that?" Kartik said on Cricbuzz.He also questioned why only three players were held responsible for the incident, arguing that the bowlers would have been informed if the plan was intended to help them."I was surprised that only three guys had to bear the brunt of it. Everybody, all the bowlers, would've known. When you're trying to do something for the sake of the bowlers, wouldn't you tell the bowlers? How can anyone believe that? Are we in kindergarten to accept that sort of thing? There have been so many murmurs: 'Oh, Warner is going to come out with a tell-all. Warner is going to tell the story once he is done with everything. ' It's not him, it's Usman Khawaja who has come out and said that everybody knew. I am pretty sure everybody knew," he added.The debate has also drawn a fresh response from former Australia opener David Warner , who accused Cricket Australia (CA) of covering up details of the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.Warner, who received a one-year ban for his role in the incident, questioned the governing body's investigation, claiming that it did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Starc or Nathan Lyon."As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," he said on Instagram."If that's correct then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?"It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea."That stinks of a cover-up."The controversy returned to the spotlight this week after Khawaja released his autobiography, in which he alleged that the entire team knew about the plan to use sandpaper to rough up the ball and make it swing.Cricket Australia's investigation at the time concluded that only then-captain Steve Smith, his deputy Warner and Cameron Bancroft knew about the plan. All three were sent home from South Africa following the incident.Cummins addressed Khawaja's claims during a lengthy press conference on Friday, describing them as "100 percent wrong". Warner subsequently accused the Australia captain of throwing his close friend Khawaja "under the bus".
Article Summary: Former India spinner Murali Kartik has backed Usman Khawaja in the ongoing debate over the 2018 ball-tampering scandal. Kartik questioned Pat Cummins'claim that he was unaware of the plan to use sandpaper during the Cape Town Test against South Africa. Former Australia opener David Warner has accused Cricket Australia of covering up details of the scandal.

Article Title: Portugal plan special Ronaldo tribute: Entire squad to wear No. 7 shirts, Denmark game to pause in seventh minute
Article Text:
FILE - Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo prepares to kick a penalty during a round of sixteen match between Portugal and Slovenia at the Euro 2024 soccer tournament in Frankfurt, Germany, Monday, July 1, 2024. (AP Photo/Matthias Schrader, File)

Portugal players to wear Cristiano Ronaldo's No. 7 shirt against Denmark

Jorge Jesus explains who organised Portugal's farewell to Ronaldo

Cristiano Ronaldo's Portugal records after 23 years and 146 goals

FILE - Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo gestures as he holds the trophy while celebrating winning the UEFA Nations League final soccer match between Portugal and Netherlands at the Dragao stadium in Porto, Portugal. AP/PTI(AP11_05_2026_000313B)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Portugal are preparing a series of tributes to Cristiano Ronaldo when they face Denmark in the UEFA Nations League on Saturday, marking the end of an international career that lasted more than two decades. The Portuguese Football Federation has approved a collective gesture involving every player in the squad, while supporters at the Estadio Municipal de Braga will also have an opportunity to honour their former captain during the match.The most visible part of the tribute will come before kick-off, when every member of Portugal's squad is expected to wear the No. 7 shirt associated with Ronaldo as the team walks out at the Estadio Municipal de Braga.The decision was reportedly finalised during a meeting on Thursday involving Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) president Pedro Proença, national team head coach Jorge Jesus and the senior leadership group. The players involved in the discussions included captains Bernardo Silva, Rúben Dias and Bruno Fernandes.According to Portuguese newspaper A Bola , the meeting brought together the federation's leadership and coaching staff to determine how best to recognise Ronaldo's contribution following his announcement of international retirement on November 5.The tribute will extend beyond the pre-match walk-out. The match is also scheduled to be paused in the seventh minute, allowing supporters to rise and applaud the former captain. UEFA has reportedly granted special permission for the gesture, giving fans at the Braga stadium an opportunity to recognise the player whose number has become synonymous with Portuguese football.Ronaldo's attendance remains unconfirmed, so it is not yet clear whether he will be present to witness the ceremony himself.Jesus addressed the arrangements during his pre-match press conference, making clear that the tribute was a decision taken by the federation rather than one organised independently by the coaching staff.“Such decisions are always the responsibility of the Portuguese Football Federation, more specifically its football and sporting departments and its president,” Jesus said.The Portugal coach also spoke about the scale of Ronaldo's contribution, pointing to the 23 years he spent representing the national team and the influence he had beyond the country.“It is brilliant because nobody can forget the 23 years Cris spent with the national team, what he achieved for Portugal, and the impact he has had on the world of football,” Jesus added.The federation has also decided to leave vacant the room Ronaldo used at Cidade do Futebol, Portugal's national team training complex. The gesture is intended to preserve a symbolic place for the former captain within the squad during the first international break following his retirement.The arrangements come as Portugal begin preparing for a future without the player who has been central to their national team for much of the modern era. Bruno Fernandes and Bernardo Silva are among the experienced figures expected to assume greater leadership responsibilities, although Ronaldo's departure leaves a significant gap in both the squad's history and its attacking record.Ronaldo retired from international football with 146 goals in 234 appearances, records that leave him as the leading goalscorer and most-capped player in the history of men's international football.His Portugal debut came on August 20, 2003, against Kazakhstan, beginning a career that concluded on September 24, 2026. Across those 23 years, he became the defining figure of a generation that delivered the country's first European Championship title and two Nations League triumphs.Portugal's victory at Euro 2016 in France was the defining achievement of Ronaldo's international career, followed by Nations League titles in 2019 and 2025. His individual records extended across both major international competitions: he scored 11 goals in 27 World Cup appearances, making him Portugal's leading scorer at the tournament, and established the men's record of 14 goals in European Championship final tournaments.He also became the only player to score at six different men's World Cups, finding the net in Germany in 2006, South Africa in 2010, Brazil in 2014, Russia in 2018, Qatar in 2022 and the 2026 tournament. His combined total of 25 goals across the European Championship and World Cup is another men's international record.Ronaldo scored against 49 different national teams, with Luxembourg conceding 11 goals and Hungary nine. His international record also includes 10 hat-tricks, two of which contained four goals, and 22 converted penalties. Of his 146 goals, 124 came in competitive internationals, excluding friendly matches.Those numbers provide the statistical measure of a career that also included unsuccessful campaigns and difficult tournament exits before Portugal's major successes. The tribute against Denmark will give the federation, the players and supporters an opportunity to recognise the full contribution of a footballer whose influence extended well beyond the records he accumulated.
Article Summary: Portugal preparing a series of tributes to Cristiano Ronaldo when they face Denmark in the UEFA Nations League on Saturday. The Portuguese Football Federation has approved a collective gesture involving every player in the squad. The most visible part of the tribute will come before kick-off, when every member of Portugal's squad is expected to wear the No. 7 shirt associated with Ronaldo. UEFA has reportedly granted special permission for the gesture. The match is also scheduled to be paused in the seventh minute, allowing supporters to rise and applaud the former captain.

Article Title: PT Usha keeps fight alive, re-enters IOA election fray via National Sports Federation route
Article Text:
PT Usha (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: PT Usha has refused to leave the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) presidential race without waging one last fight. After losing out on a direct entry into the IOA General Assembly by finishing fifth in Monday’s contentious Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) elections and missing the four women’s places, Usha has found an unlikely ally in the the Ice Hockey Association of India (IHAI), as their women’s representative.Adopting the National Sports Federation (NSF) route, Usha is the IHAI’s women’s nominee in the provisional electoral college for the IOA Executive Council (EC) elections on Dec 5, released by electoral officer Sanjay K Srivastava on Thursday. Harjinder Singh is the association’s male nominee. The move is a pointed response to those who believed her SOM defeat had ended her bid for a second term as IOA chief.The SOM setback had triggered a protest from Usha. She lodged four complaints with the electoral officer over alleged campaigning by incumbent officials, messages seeking confirmation of voters’ participation and references to the sports ministry. In a Nov 9 letter to International Olympic Committee (IOC) president Kirsty Coventry, she sought an independent examination and asked whether govt or external influence had been exerted.The provisional list has its own flashpoints. At the All India Tennis Association (AITA), interim president Chintan Parikh and Rushmi Chakravarthi figure as representatives, but IOA’s current EC member Rohit Rajpal is missing.Rajpal has objected, alleging Parikh bypassed an AITA executive committee meeting and secured approval through an advisory group. He questioned why Leander Paes was not included and Parikh’s name sent instead. Both Rajpal and Parikh are contesting AITA’s elections on Nov 27 as presidential hopefuls.Another issue is at the Indian Weightlifting Federation (IWLF), where its president Sahdev Yadav has nominated himself as male representative and his wife, Sabina Yadav, as the female nominee.Former Athletics Federation of India (AFI) chief Adille Sumariwalla, who withdrew from the SOM contest, is back alongside Jyotirmoyee Sikdar, and remains an aspiring canidate for IOA’s top post. Former IOA secretary general Rajeev Mehta and NRAI’s Ajay Patel also feature, signalling an old-guard return.Hockey India’s list includes secretary general Bhola Nath Singh and Joydeep Kaur, but not HI president Dilip Tirkey, amid the power struggle for control of the federation between Singh and Tirkey. AIFF has nominated president Kalyan Chaubey, while the handball federation has proposed Udit Sheth, whose Yogasana Bharat recognition was quashed by the Delhi High Court.The final electoral roll will be published on Nov 15 after scrutiny and withdrawals. It will also include eight elected SOMs and India’s IOC member.
Article Summary: PT Usha has found an unlikely ally in the the Ice Hockey Association of India (IHAI), as their women’s representative. The move is a pointed response to those who believed her SOM defeat had ended her bid for a second term as IOA chief. She lodged four complaints with the electoral officer over alleged campaigning.

Article Title: Rs 50 lakh debt, visa nightmare: Teenage Indian chess prodigy risks losing US scholarship
Article Text:
IM Md Imran (Special Arrangements)

The Bratislava incident that changed everything

A university dream on hold

A family stretched to its financial limits

A race against time

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

One final Grandmaster norm

Funchal Open, Portugal: November 26 to December 2

El Llobregat Open, Spain: December 3 to 8

Sunway Sitges Chess Festival, Spain: December 12 to 22

Rilton Cup, Stockholm, Sweden: December 27 to January 5

NEW DELHI: Last June, seventeen-year-old Md Imran was in Bratislava, Slovakia, when an incident turned his European chess campaign into a nightmare. As previously reported on TimesofIndia.com , he lost his passport, his phone, money and several personal belongings. More than just his valuables, he had lost something far more important, his valid US F-1 visa and Schengen visa.Stranded in a foreign country, with no easy way to get home or continue his journey, the young Indian chess player suddenly found himself fighting a battle that had little to do with the 64 squares. But Imran, hailing from Andhra Pradesh, refused to let the setback end his journey.In the days and weeks that followed, he produced two consecutive Grandmaster (GM) norms, bringing him within touching distance of the coveted Grandmaster title.Yet, four months after that incident, Imran is back in India, facing a different kind of situation, which includes an unresolved US visa crisis, mounting family debt, and the possibility of losing a full university scholarship that could change his life.The teenager, who became an International Master (IM) in 2025, has already deferred his admission to the University of Texas at Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) in Brownsville, Texas, from Fall 2026 to Spring 2027.His new university orientation is scheduled for January 19, 2027. If he cannot secure his US F-1 visa before then, he risks losing the scholarship altogether.For a teenager who has spent years travelling across continents to chase his Grandmaster dream, the next few months could prove decisive.The consequences of losing his passport in Bratislava were particularly severe because it contained both his valid US F-1 visa and his Schengen visa, which was valid until October 31.He eventually managed to obtain a replacement passport from the Indian Embassy in Budapest on June 29 and returned to India on July 6. But coming home did not mean the troubles were over."The very next day, on July 7th, I applied for a new Schengen visa for Hungary. This marked my 13th attempt at applying for a Schengen visa," Imran told TimesofIndia.com.Despite having competed extensively in Hungary over the previous two years, and having previously received a one-year multiple-entry visa from the same consulate, Imran was granted only a three-month visa, valid from July 18 to October 31.The decision left him frustrated, particularly when he knew fellow players who had received visas valid for two to five years in far fewer attempts."It sounded completely ridiculous, especially when I know many friends who have received 2- to 5-year validity visas in just their 2nd to 5th attempts. I truly don't understand what's wrong with my case," he added.For a young professional chess player, travelling back to India solely to process visas means more than another appointment and a few documents."Flying back to India solely for visa processing costs an exorbitant amount of time and heavy money on flight tickets, on top of the constant re-application hurdles," he added.Even amid the uncertainty, Imran had already earned two norms in closed round-robin tournaments and was chasing his final open Swiss GM norm to complete the requirements for the Grandmaster title.His original plan was to continue competing in Europe, secure the remaining norm and return to India in time to obtain a US visa and attend UTRGV's Fall 2026 student orientation on August 23. But the US visa appointment never materialised."I waited in Europe and tried for a U.S. appointment all the way through August, September, and October. Unfortunately, despite trying every single day for four months since the June incident, I still have not secured an appointment," he said.With the August university deadline passing, he had little choice but to defer his admission to Spring 2027.His scholarship remains at stake. If he cannot make it to the university by the January 19 orientation, he could lose the financial support that would help him pursue higher education alongside his chess career.Between July and October, he competed in over ten events. However, only three were strong open tournaments where he had a realistic opportunity to secure his final GM norm.The remaining events were regular prize-money opens and round-robin competitions that helped him stay active.The three major opportunities were also poorly spaced, with two tournaments scheduled back-to-back between August 8 and 23, followed by the final one from October 3 to 11.It was a relentless schedule, made even harder by the uncertainty surrounding his university admission and his inability to secure a US visa appointment.The pressure eventually took its toll on the chessboard."Under the intense psychological pressure of the missing norm and my crumbling U.S. visa situation, my performance dipped. I suffered an insane rating decline despite relentless fighting spirit. Completely exhausted and under immense stress, I flew back home on October 12," Imran, who had a peak rating of 2503 and is now rated 2477, revealed.Imran's father is a police officer, while his mother is a homemaker. Coming from a middle-class background, the family has had to stretch its resources to support his international chess career.Playing professionally in Europe costs between Rs 1.5 lakh and Rs 3 lakh every month. The expenses include flights, visas, accommodation, tournament entry fees, food and travel between countries.The family has reportedly accumulated loans of around Rs 40-50 lakh to finance his career. The June incident in Slovakia added another unexpected financial burden, with the loss of his passport, phone and other valuables."My father has supported me with everything he possibly can, stretching himself to the absolute limit, but it's falling short over time," Imran further noted. "I built my chess career entirely through my own hard work without formal high-end coaching."Imran has approached the Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister's Office and other political leaders, seeking financial assistance through state sports incentive schemes. However, his requests have so far gone unanswered.With his three-month Schengen visa approaching its October 31 expiry, Imran returned to the Hungarian Consulate in Mumbai on October 16 for another application. It was his 14th Schengen visa application.This time, he received an emergency appointment and was granted a one-year visa on October 24. While the longer validity offers some relief, it was still shorter than the five-year visa he had hoped to secure given his extensive tournament and travel history across Europe.At least one part of the travel crisis had eased. But the bigger problem remained untouched, his US F-1 visa. With January 19, 2027, approaching, Imran now needs to secure an appointment and complete the visa process in time to join UTRGV and protect his scholarship.Despite everything, Imran is preparing to return to Europe for another demanding tournament circuit in the hope of securing his final GM norm. He is scheduled to fly back on November 19, with four events lined up across Portugal, Spain and Sweden:The schedule leaves little room for rest. More importantly, he is desperately hoping to secure a US visa appointment before leaving India on November 19."My life is currently at a critical crossroads. Between the heavy financial debts of playing professional chess, the constant struggle to secure my final GM norm, and the looming threat of losing my U.S. university scholarship at the University of Texas at Rio Grande Valley if I can't resolve my visa crisis by Spring 2027, the situation is completely overwhelming," he concluded.For a teenager who has done so much to keep his dreams alive, the question is whether the support he needs will arrive before January 19.
Article Summary: Indian chess player Md Imran was in Bratislava, Slovakia, when an incident turned his European chess campaign into a nightmare. He lost his passport, his phone, money and several personal belongings. He also lost his valid US F-1 visa and Schengen visa. Four months after that incident, Imran is back in India, facing a different kind of situation, which includes an unresolved US visa crisis.

Article Title: ‘Very disappointed’: IOC backs call for clean IOA elections after Usha flags SOM poll irregularities; warns of damage to India’s Olympic reputation
Article Text:
PT Usha (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has stepped into the raging Indian Olympic Association (IOA) election controversy, expressing strong displeasure over the recurring disputes surrounding its electoral process and warning that the developments are damaging the reputation of the Olympic movement in India.In a strongly worded communication to IOA president PT Usha on her complaints, the world body has called for elections to be conducted in strict compliance with the Olympic Charter and IOA Constitution, in a “free and fair manner and without any external interference”.The IOC's letter to Usha, in the exclusive possession of TOI, comes in the wake of the IOA president's Nov 9 communication to IOC president Kirsty Coventry, in which she sought an independent examination of alleged irregularities in the contentious Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) elections. The latest communication, signed by James Macleod, Director, NOC Relations, Olympic Solidarity and Olympism365, has also been marked to IOC member Nita Ambani and the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA).Opening with an unambiguous expression of displeasure, Macleod wrote: “In response to the complaints and media reports that have been brought to our attention over the past few days, we would like to express the IOC’s position as follows.”The IOC then made its disappointment explicit, stating: “The IOC is very disappointed to note that, once again, issues and disputes seem to have resurfaced in the conduct of the IOA election process and in the implementation of the rules governing the IOA elections, despite all the efforts made over the past few years to establish a strong governance framework for the IOA in accordance with the Olympic Charter and the Basic Principles of Good Governance within the Olympic Movement. ”In perhaps its strongest observation, the IOC warned that the controversy was having consequences beyond the IOA's internal power struggle. “This extremely regrettable situation is, once again, negatively affecting the operations and reputation of the Olympic Movement in India,” the letter stated.The IOC's intervention assumes significance against the backdrop of Usha's detailed complaint to Coventry. In her three-page communication, the IOA president had flagged alleged campaigning by incumbent officials, WhatsApp messages soliciting votes for a particular panel, communications seeking confirmation of voters' participation and references to the sports ministry during an election involving a secret ballot.She had also questioned the handling of four representations submitted to electoral officer Sanjay K. Srivastava and sought an independent examination of whether government or external influence had been exerted.Usha had maintained that her complaint was not an attempt to challenge the result simply because she had lost, but was about the conduct and oversight of the electoral process and the need to protect the autonomy of the IOA.The IOC has now directly addressed the responsibility of those conducting the elections. “We urge the IOA and the Electoral Officer directly responsible for the IOA election process to ensure that the IOA elections can be conducted in full compliance with the Olympic Charter, the IOA Constitution, and all applicable rules, in a free and fair manner and without any external interference,” Macleod wrote.The letter further stressed: “We sincerely count on everyone's collaboration to ensure that the above is strictly respected, in order to avoid any unnecessary complications and further escalation.” It also requested that a copy be sent to the relevant government authorities.The controversy erupted after Usha finished fifth with 40 votes in the six-way contest for four women's SOM positions on November 9. Anju Bobby George topped the poll with 53 votes, followed by Rani Rampal (50), Dola Banerjee (45) and Saina Nehwal (43).While the IOC has not adjudicated Usha's specific allegations or named anyone responsible for the reported violations, its unequivocal warning puts the IOA's electoral administration under international scrutiny.With the executive council elections scheduled for Dec 5, the message is unmistakable: the process must command credibility, follow the rules and remain free from external interference.
Article Summary: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has stepped into the raging Indian Olympic Association (IOA) election controversy. In a strongly worded communication to IOA president PT Usha on her complaints, the world body has called for elections to be conducted in strict compliance with the Olympic Charter and IOA Constitution. The IOC warned that the controversy was having consequences beyond the IOA's internal power struggle.

Article Title: Vivaan Kapoor clinches trap silver, LA quota
Article Text:
Vivaan Kapoor

Pune:

TOI

There was history riding on Vivaan Kapoor as he competed for gold in the men’s trap event at the ISSF World Championships in Doha on Thursday. The Jaipur shooter fell short of gold but still made history, winning silver and an Olympic quota place for the Los Angeles Games.At 24, Vivaan became the fourth Indian to win a World Championships medal in trap and the second, after Dr Karni Singh, to claim silver. Manavjit Singh Sandhu remains the only Indian to have won gold in the event. Zoravar Singh Sandhu’s bronze is India’s other trap medal at the Worlds.It was also the first time two Indians reached a trap final at the World Championships. Udaivir Singh Jaijee joined Vivaan in the eight-man final and finished sixth.Vivaan was in excellent form in the final, hitting 29 of 30 clays. He was tied with Kuwait’s Abdulrahman Alfaihan as the contest went to a shoot-off. Vivaan looked strong, but Alfaihan held his nerve and beat him by one shot, winning the shoot-off 3-2.The final featured a strong field, including Paris Games gold medallist Nathan Hales and silver medallist Ying Qi of China. Qi took bronze with 22 hits, while Hales was eliminated in fifth place with 11.Udaivir finished with 11 hits.“I was a little nervous, but I managed to hold my nerve. I didn’t put pressure on myself during the shoot-offs because I’ve had a lot of shoot-off practice with our coach Peter Wilson in training. I followed my routine and tried to do my best,” Vivaan toldFor Wilson, the result will help Indian shooters build confidence for future tournaments.“Two Indians in the Worlds final and both doing well—this was unheard of. But now everybody will start believing that this is achievable. I said more than six months ago that Indian trap shooters would achieve success soon. We saw Neeru win World Cup gold, then Asian gold, and now Vivaan has won silver and a quota place,” said Wilson, India’s foreign coach and a gold medallist at the 2012 London Games.Earlier, in the qualification round, Vivaan and Udaivir were among seven shooters tied on 120. They competed in a shoot-off for four available places, and both advanced to the top eight. With Vivaan’s achievement, India has recorded its best World Championships showing, winning three medals and three quota places in one edition. The country’s previous best tally was two, achieved ahead of the Paris and Tokyo Games.
Article Summary: Vivaan Kapoor wins silver in the men's trap event at the ISSF World Championships in Doha. The 24-year-old becomes the fourth Indian to win a World Championships medal in trap and the second, after Dr Karni Singh, to claim silver. It was also the first time two Indians reached a trap final at the World Championships.

That week we were in our home in Kodagu, a little away from Madikeri town. By the time I returned from my morning walk that day (Oct 28), our neighbours in Bengaluru had called my wife to inform her about a break-in at our place.My first thought was about my medals, especially the 1980 Moscow Olympics gold, because those were the only precious items which I felt we had left at home. As my wife drove us to Bengaluru, I spent much of the journey calling my niece and then the police, who put me at ease by telling me not to panic.As the police worked on collecting fingerprints and other forensic evidence, I kept asking my family who had gone in what they could actually see. The medal boxes were there, they said, but the medals were missing. I hoped they were under the pile of clothes those people had strewn and left behind.My heart sank when I walked into the house. First, at all the clothes all around the place, then at the broken cupboard lock. The empty boxes of medals made me feel very sad and disappointed because I cherished them so much; they carried so many good memories and sentiments, and to me, they will always be priceless.I remember when I came back from Moscow, people often asked about the medal. But over time, fewer people asked to see it. Maybe the importance of Olympic sports had declined as other sports took over, but somehow, all that didn't matter at this moment.My worst fear was losing the medals and never seeing them again. And that would have been a big blow because they were the only prize we received for winning and participating in the Olympics at Moscow. I felt a great dread that I wouldn't get them back and that they wouldn't be recovered.As I have said before, I thought the people who took it away likely didn't know its sporting value. For me, it was priceless, for them, it was gold. It could end up at a pawn shop or worse, just be melted down. That thought gnawed away inside me.Despite the sinking feeling, I immediately began running other scenarios through my mind - whether I could apply to the International Olympic Committee for a replacement medal because of the loss. At the same time, there was that smidgen of hope that lingered because the police had given me their assurance.In the two weeks between the break-in and Wednesday's recovery, I was assailed by a lot of nostalgia. The day we won the medal, Zafar Iqbal and I were taken for a dope test immediately after the medal ceremony. Once back in the Games Village, I was so exhausted that I slept without changing. The medal had stayed around my neck! Other memories played out as well.I thought back with gratitude because that was my first time playing for India. Also, I had never been out of the country. I had never played on artificial turf before. I looked back at the youngster in me, who wore an oversized India kit (I was a thin boy) and went out to play.Days with our coach, Balkrishan Singh, and captain V Baskaran came back to me, and recollections of how they had faith in me and guided me. I wasn't in the initial playing XI and was one of the two substitutes, more like an understudy. Just before the Olympics, we played a few practice matches against the local clubs, and Balkrishan sir and Baskaran felt I should be in the playing XI, which I'd never dreamt I would be in. It's where my career took off. The trust they showed in me meant I probably never sat on the bench for almost nine years that followed.
Article Summary: MM Somaya is an 1980 Olympic gold medallist and 1982 Asian Games silver medalist. His medals were stolen during a break-in at his home in Kodagu, Karnataka. The medals were the only prize we received for winning and participating in the Olympics at Moscow.

Legendary India batter Sunil Gavaskar has weighed in on the debate surrounding Virat Kohli 's pursuit of 100 international centuries, suggesting that a teammate making a personal sacrifice to help the star reach the landmark would bring joy to Indian cricket fans as well.Kohli was in superb touch during the first ODI against New Zealand, smashing 74 off just 51 deliveries to guide India towards victory in a low-scoring contest. However, Gavaskar raised an interesting possibility in his latest column for: had Kohli stayed at the crease for longer, captain Shubman Gill and vice-captain Shreyas Iyer could have found themselves in a difficult position.With India closing in on the target, the two batters might have had to choose between finishing the match quickly and giving Kohli an opportunity to reach his century. The prospect becomes even more significant given that Kohli is chasing the historic mark of 100 international hundreds.Gavaskar acknowledged that winning a match must remain the team's primary objective, but argued that helping a player achieve such a landmark, provided it does not compromise the result, could be a moment of collective celebration."Indians have always been fond of records and so there's always a debate about the rights and wrongs of going for it.One thing for sure that 99% of those who say they don't play for records are actually incapable talent and temperament wise of setting any and so it's easy for them to say so," Gavaskar wrote."There is not a single Indian cricket fan who does not want Kohli to get to 100 international centuries. We are all cheering for him to get there and so, if there's an occasion where some other teammate sacrifices his runs to allow him the chance to get there, the glory will not be just Kohli's but for all Indian cricket fans too," he added.Kohli eventually fell for 74 with India at 124/3 in the rain-affected contest, leaving the team with relatively little work to do in the chase. His dismissal also meant Gill and Iyer did not have to confront the possibility of managing the chase around his personal milestone.Gavaskar felt the two players were spared a potentially awkward situation, including the prospect of facing criticism from fans on social media if India had delayed sealing the victory to give Kohli a chance to complete his hundred."Kohli got out in the 70s. Gill and Iyer were thus spared any blowback if the winning runs had been hit with Kohli unbeaten in the 90s. Yes, it's a team game, but it's also good for the team if one of its members, especially a star player, gets to a personal milestone without affecting the team's chances of winning," Gavaskar pointed out.Kohli, who now plays only ODIs, has 86 international centuries to his name. He is chasing a landmark that remains exclusive to Sachin Tendulkar, the only batter to have scored 100 international hundreds.
Article Summary: Virat Kohli is chasing the historic mark of 100 international hundreds. Sunil Gavaskar says a teammate making a personal sacrifice to help the star reach the landmark would bring joy to Indian cricket fans as well. Kohli was in superb touch during the first ODI against New Zealand, smashing 74.

Article Title: ‘He got greedy’: Ex-India captain's blunt take on Arshdeep Singh after four-wicket haul
Article Text:

Jadeja impressed with Anshul Kamboj

Former India cricketer Ajay Jadeja has praised Arshdeep Singh's overall performance in India's five-wicket victory over New Zealand in the first ODI in Auckland, but believes the left-arm pacer could have avoided an expensive finish to his spell.India began their five-match ODI series with a comfortable win at Eden Park on Wednesday, November 4. In a rain-interrupted contest reduced to 32 overs per side, New Zealand were bowled out for 185 before India chased down the revised target of 143 in just 22.4 overs. Virat Kohli led the chase with a fluent 74, while Shubman Gill contributed 37 as the duo stitched together a 113-run partnership. India eventually crossed the finish line with five wickets to spare and 56 deliveries remaining.With the ball, Arshdeep was India's leading wicket-taker, claiming four wickets in his 10 overs. However, his figures of 4/70 were inflated by an expensive final over in which New Zealand tailender Blair Tickner struck him for three sixes, taking 23 runs off the over.Assessing the pacer's performance, Jadeja felt Arshdeep had been impressive for most of his spell but allowed the opportunity to complete a five-wicket haul to influence his bowling towards the end."I would call him slightly greedy. He himself said that as well. If you remove his last over, he had dismissed four batters before that and had given 40-odd runs. He got slightly greedy for the fifth wicket in the last over," Jadeja said on Sony Sports Network.Arshdeep had himself admitted after the match that the fifth wicket would have been his favourite, indicating that he was keen to complete a five-wicket haul. Despite missing out on the milestone, his four-wicket effort placed him in an exclusive group of Indian fast bowlers to achieve the feat in an ODI in New Zealand, alongside Javagal Srinath and Mohammed Shami.Jadeja, however, stressed that the expensive final over should not overshadow what Arshdeep brings to India's bowling combination. He pointed to the value of having a left-arm fast bowler in an attack that already features Jasprit Bumrah, adding that the competition for places would only benefit the team."It happens. It's natural, but Arshdeep Singh is showing that he can play in ODIs as well, which I believe is a very good thing when a left-arm seamer gets added to this attack with (Jasprit) Bumrah. The competition has increased a lot, which is very good for India," Jadeja elaborated.Jadeja also reserved praise for Anshul Kamboj, who delivered an economical spell of 2/22 from his 10 overs and walked away with the Player of the Match award.The former India batter acknowledged that Kamboj had faced questions over his bowling during his Test debut against England in 2025, particularly regarding his pace and tendency to bowl no-balls. However, he felt the youngster had shown considerable improvement in Auckland.Jadeja also suggested that Kamboj's workload before the England assignment could have contributed to his struggles, pointing out that fatigue can affect a bowler's execution. His performance against New Zealand, according to Jadeja, reflected better pace, consistency and accuracy."He bowled extremely well. The vision everyone had was that he didn't have pace when he played in England and was bowling a lot of no-balls. I think he had come after playing a lot of cricket then. So a guy also gets tired. It's not that easy. Then he was playing for the first time, but the consistency and the slight increase in his pace he showed today (Wednesday), if we talk about the accuracy amongst the four bowlers, it's Anshul Kamboj," Jadeja added.
Article Summary: India beat New Zealand by five wickets in the first ODI in Auckland. Ajay Jadeja praised Arshdeep Singh's performance, but said he could have avoided expensive final over. Jadeja also praised Anshul Kamboj's bowling, saying he had shown improvement.

Article Title: ‘More people had known’: Sandpapergate reviewer reveals whispers of wider ball-tampering scandal
Article Text:

Dr Simon Longstaff, the ethics expert commissioned by Cricket Australia (CA) to review the team's culture after the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal, has revealed that he heard “whispers” that more players knew about the ball-tampering plot than the three who were punished.Speaking to Nine's Weekend Today on Saturday, Longstaff said he gave senior players an opportunity to reveal anything they had not disclosed during the investigation, but nobody changed their statements.“Along the way, there were whispers, and I can't put it any more strongly than that, that something else had gone on earlier and that more people had known,” he said.“When we came to look into that – because I couldn’t turn a blind eye to it once the suggestion was made – I afforded the senior people I spoke with an opportunity … ‘Well, is there something else you want to say about the whole circumstance?’”“Nobody chose to make any alteration to their statement, so I was left with basically a blank wall. Some people saying one thing, others another, but not sufficient to be able to say there needs to be a further inquiry at that time,” he added.Longstaff said the whispers also suggested that ball-tampering may have taken place before the infamous Cape Town Test against South Africa.“We’re talking effectively about … good people who made bad decisions, so that’s where we looked,” he said.He could not recall whether Usman Khawaja was invited to contribute to the review, after the former Australia opener claimed in his book, Sabr, that he was never interviewed despite being willing to tell his version of events.“I can't remember exactly who it was that was given the opportunity to contribute to our review, which went much further than just the players involved,” Longstaff said.“It looked at the whole of Cricket Australia, sponsors, supporters … past Test players to see what the comparison could be. Not everybody we invited to participate in our review chose to accept that invitation. They had the liberty not to.”Longstaff also said contributions were made under strict confidentiality conditions.On Pat Cummins ' denial of Khawaja's claims, Longstaff described the Australia captain's press conference as “absolutely convincing in his sincerity”.“If Cummins did not know, and I believe he didn't, then not everybody knew. But that leaves a different question,” he said, adding that it remained unclear whether a considerably larger group knew about the plan.He suggested CA should decide whether it wanted to establish the reason behind the conflicting accounts.Meanwhile, David Warner has accused CA of conducting a flawed investigation and questioned whether it interviewed senior bowlers Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon “As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation,” Warner posted on Instagram.“If that’s correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn’t know?”“It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea. That stinks of a cover up.”Warner and then captain Steve Smith received one-year bans, while Cameron Bancroft was suspended for nine months following the Cape Town incident.
Article Summary: Dr Simon Longstaff has revealed that he heard 'whispers' that more players knew about the ball-tampering plot than the three who were punished. Longstaff said he gave senior players an opportunity to reveal anything they had not disclosed during the investigation, but nobody changed their statements. He could not recall whether Usman Khawaja was invited to contribute to the review.

MUMBAI: India women’s cricket team head coach Amol Muzumdar urged young cricketers to respect the game, embrace failure and put the team first at the Times Cricket Shield prize distribution function at the MCA Lounge, Wankhede Stadium, on Friday.Recalling his early days in Mumbai cricket, Muzumdar spoke about the advice he received from former India batter and 1983 World Cup winner Sandeep Patil when he made his Times Shield debut for Sungrace Mafatlal in 1993. The Times Award Shield was sponsored by The Times of India Cricket Shield’s celebration partner Heineken 0.0 (Mr. Vasant Bhandari) and Sterling Reserve Packaged Drinking Water. Incidentally, this is the 96th year of the Times Shield, which started in 1930.“Score 200. What’s the big deal about scoring 100? Everyone here scores hundreds. If you have the guts, score a double hundred, then I’ll accept it,” Patil had told him. The words motivated the then 18-year-old, but his debut innings ended at 97. “As I was walking back, the captain was sitting in front of me. He gave me a smirk. That was my baptism of fire in Mumbai cricket,” Muzumdar recalled.Three months later, he scored a then world-record 260 on his firstclass debut for Mumbai against Haryana in a Ranji Trophy pre-quarterfinal in Feb 1994.Muzumdar, who went on to captain Mumbai and score 11,167 runs in 171 first-class matches, offered three lessons to youngsters.“Respect the game. That is the most important thing. The game will respect you back multifold,” he said.He also urged players not to fear failure. “Failures are part of every cricketer’s life, it’s only a question of how you respond,” he said.Highlighting the importance of the Times Shield in Mumbai cricket, Muzumdar said, “The Times Shield has been an integral part of Mumbai cricket. But I can tell you one thing: It was an absolute privilege to play in the Times Cricket Shield when I first started. It’s not just a tournament, but an institution. It is probably the livelihood of so many cricketers. It gave a platform, an encouragement to so many cricketers to display their talent.“It was just an honour to play in the Times Shield when I started and even when I finished in 2013.” Former India batter and BCCI Cricket Advisory Committee member Jatin Paranjape, the other chief guest, lauded the tournament’s role in strengthening Mumbai’s club cricket.

CHENNAI: At a time when Australian cricket could do with some good news, 21-year-old Mahli Beardman provided a glimmer of hope. The young fast bowler made an extraordinary impression on his ODI debut, claiming 6/24 in 7.4 overs to dismantle England on a lively Perth pitch in the series opener.England were bundled out for 131 in 33.4 overs, with Australia subsequently chasing down the target in 23.3 overs to seal a convincing win and take a 1-0 lead in the three-match ODI series. Beardman recorded the best bowling figures by an Australian on ODI debut and the fourth-best overall. He also needed just 28 deliveries to complete his five-wicket haul, the fastest by an Australian in the format.The young right-arm fast bowler has grown up admiring two fast-bowling greats — Mitchell Johnson and Dale Steyn. There was a familiar aggression to the performance, in addition to the knack of trying to pitch the ball up and inducing the edge. He got dismissed Harry Brook and Joe Root with deliveries that got the edges and followed it up with short-pitched stuff as well that completely dismantled the English line-up.It was in Oct that Beardman was going all guns blazing in Puducherry for Australia ‘A’, setting up a series win in the 50-over format. During the tour, when TOI caught up with Beardman, the pacer said: “Johnson’s 2013-14 Ashes campaign against England left a huge impression on me.Watching him bowl with that aggression really fuelled my interest in fast bowling. Steyn was my favourite. I followed him closely growing up and even tried to replicate his bowling action. Those two were my biggest inspirations,” Beardman said.Beardman values the opportunity to learn from Australia’s celebrated pace trio of Pat Cummins , Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc , having already picked their brains during previous assignments. “Bowling alongside them would be a fantastic opportunity. Starc has been particularly generous with his advice, while Pat and Josh have also been helpful whenever I’ve had the chance to interact with them,” he said.Australia 132-3 in 23.3 overs (M Marsh 50) beat England 131 in 33.4 overs (M Beardman 6-24, S Johnson 3-42) by seven wickets.

Pakistan head coach Mike Hesson has called for the use of the pink ball in day Test matches at home to be seriously considered after rain and poor light disrupted the opening Test against Sri Lanka in Rawalpindi, which ended in a draw with nearly 141 overs lost.Hesson and Pakistan captain Babar Azam are open to the idea of using the pink ball in future home Test series, particularly during the winter months when weather conditions make it difficult to complete scheduled playing hours.The opening Test was repeatedly interrupted by bad light, forcing players to leave the field before the scheduled close of play on most days. The fourth day was called off during the afternoon session because of rain.Even before the rain arrived on the fourth day, umpires had to suspend play because the light had deteriorated to a level where continuing with the red ball under lights could have put players at risk of injury.The match was already heading towards a draw when play resumed on the fifth day. Pakistan were leading by just 45 runs with one wicket down as they looked to build a target for Sri Lanka.Pakistan ended up batting through the day before play was called off at 4:18 pm, almost two hours before the scheduled close at 6:10 pm.The decision came after Saud Shakeel was dismissed in the 90s for the second time in the match.The first three days had also seen significant interruptions, with only 14.2, 15.1 and 12 overs bowled in the evening sessions respectively.The International Cricket Council (ICC), following its last quarterly meeting, has approved the use of pink balls in day Tests as an option to address the problem of overs being lost due to bad light. Hesson believes Pakistan should consider the option for future home series."It is certainly something that needs to be talked about for the future series," Hesson told the host broadcaster after the match. "It is going to be a challenge to play Test matches in this time of the year regardless of where in Pakistan. As the ICC have now allowed that to be an option, this is something that seriously needs to be considered before the series."Babar, however, pointed out that the short gap between the two Tests would not have given Pakistan enough time to prepare for a pink-ball match. With only three days between the two games, he said players needed more time to get used to the different conditions and behaviour of the pink ball."You will need to prepare for it as we usually play with the red ball," he said in the post-match presentation. "A couple of days are not enough to prepare to play a Test with the pink ball. It is a good that we have it as an option, but the preparation for a pink ball Test demands more time."

Article Title: Matt Henry's three-ball demolition exposes India's batting frailties ahead of 2027 ODI World Cup
Article Text:
Matt Henry

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Three balls. That was all Matt Henry needed to turn India’s chase of 334 into a rout.Henry was only supposed to be passing through. Having missed most of the T20Is with a leg injury and the early ODIs amid concussion concerns after colliding with Devon Conway, the seamer stayed back at Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui simply to prove his fitness and get some overs into his legs before the Tests.Instead, he produced one of the most devastating opening overs in ODI cricket, reducing India to 0/3 and setting up a 244-run thrashing — India’s second-biggest defeat by runs in the format. India collapsed for 89 and the contest was effectively sealed before the visitors had even troubled the scorers.Henry’s first ball landed on a good length on off, kicked, and seamed away just enough to square up Rohit Sharma and kiss the outside edge on its way to first slip. It was a jarring sight, painfully reminiscent of the twilight of Rohit’s Test career and an increasingly familiar one when he faces quality fast bowling in overseas conditions.Next up was Virat Kohli . Henry pitched fuller, drew him forward and beat the outside edge by inches. Three balls later, he wobbled the seam from an identical spot. This one nipped back in, stayed low and rattled Kohli’s stumps.Then came Shreyas Iyer, walking out for his captaincy debut and walking back with a golden duck — the first Indian skipper to suffer that fate. Trapped on the crease by one that darted past his inside edge, Iyer fell to a DRS review while Henry was already mid-celebration.India’s first run came off the 17th delivery of the innings.For anyone watching, it was impossible not to be dragged back to Old Trafford in July 2019, when Henry’s 3/37 ripped the heart out of India’s World Cup semifinal chase. Seven years on, the scars remain wide open.With the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa looming, where conditions could offer similar bounce and seam movement, this rout should set off alarm bells. A hint of lateral movement was all it took to expose India’s glaring technical chinks.To be fair, Henry was not operating in isolation. Kyle Jamieson used his height to extract extra bounce and movement, getting Ruturaj Gaikwad (5) to edge a feeble push outside off to second slip as India slipped to 9 for 4.Ishan Kishan (27 off 53) and Axar Patel (21 off 36) briefly resisted with a 44-run stand. Naman Dhir (21 off 24) muscled two sixes, but Matt Fisher (3 for 31) kept hitting hard lengths at high pace to snuff out any fight. Henry then returned to clean up the tail, finishing with career-best ODI figures.If India’s batting was brittle, the thinking off the field was equally baffling. On a surface offering genuine seam and bounce, leaving Mohammed Siraj out of the XI again defied cricketing logic. Gautam Gambhir’s selection calls continue to puzzle, raising serious questions about the roadmap ahead.Cruelly for India, they had walked into the innings break believing they held the momentum. After Tim Seifert (58 off 48) and Will Young forged an 85-run opening stand, Young took over and ensured there was no let-up.Dropped twice on 5 off Auqib Nabi in the second over of New Zealand’s innings, Young cashed in with a career-best 125 off 108 balls. Alongside Finn Allen (41 off 30), he took down Kuldeep Yadav (0 for 73 in 8 overs) in a 90-run fourth-wicket stand before Rohit redeemed an earlier dropped chance with a sharp diving catch at short cover.Part-timer Naman Dhir then removed Young and took a diving catch to dismiss Michael Bracewell off Gurnoor Brar. Axar (2 for 39) and Arshdeep Singh, who removed Mitchell Santner, helped India take 6 for 77 in the final 13.1 overs and bowl New Zealand out for 333.New Zealand, trailing 2-1, now head into Sunday’s final ODI without Henry and Jamieson, both bound for Test duty.
Article Summary: New Zealand beat India by 244 runs in their ODI at Bay Oval. Matt Henry took three wickets in three balls to turn India's chase into a rout. India collapsed for 89 and the contest was effectively sealed before the visitors had even troubled the scorers. Henry finished with career-best ODI figures of 3/37.

Article Title: Best ever! From 14 medals to 114: How India achieved more with fewer athletes at the Asian Para Games
Article Text:
Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

From 14 medals to 114: India's remarkable rise

India's Asian Para Games record

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Smaller contingent, bigger return

Hangzhou vs Aichi-Nagoya

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Athletics powers India's medal surge

India's leading medal-winning sports in Asian Para Games 2026

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Multiple medallists underline India's depth

Paralympic progress provides the wider context

Fourth place sets a new benchmark

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

From 14 medals in 2010 to 114 in 2026, India’s remarkable rise continued in Aichi-Nagoya as a smaller contingent surpassed its previous best, achieved 30 gold medals and secured its highest-ever finish at the continental para-sport showpiece.India’s campaign at the Asian Para Games 2026 was a triumph that few would have predicted when the size of the contingent became known. With just 167 athletes travelling to Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the prospect of repeating the 100-plus medal haul achieved at Hangzhou in 2023 appeared ambitious. The previous edition had seen India send more than 300 athletes to the competition, returning with a record 108 medals after subsequent revisions to the original tally.But the Indian contingent defied expectations, producing an even bigger return with significantly fewer athletes. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place, both the highest medal tally and the best finish in the country's history at the event.The numbers tell a compelling story of progress. India improved its medal tally for the fifth consecutive edition, added to its gold-medal record and finished ahead of South Korea, which had threatened to challenge its position in the final standings.More than the record itself, the achievement highlighted how far India's para-sport movement has travelled in 16 years — from a modest 14-medal return at the inaugural edition in 2010 to a fourth-place finish among Asia's leading para-sport nations.India's progress at the Asian Para Games has been steady, with each edition bringing a new high in the overall medal tally.At Guangzhou in 2010, India won 14 medals — one gold, four silver and nine bronze — to finish 15th. The 2014 edition in Incheon brought a substantial improvement, with the country collecting 33 medals, including three gold, but remaining 15th in the standings.The breakthrough arrived at Jakarta in 2018. India's medal tally rose to 72, comprising 15 gold, 24 silver and 33 bronze, while its position improved to ninth.Hangzhou in 2023 marked another major leap. India crossed the 100-medal barrier for the first time, initially returning with 111 medals before the tally was revised to 108 following a doping-related disqualification and a medal reallocation. The revised haul comprised 27 gold, 32 silver and 49 bronze, with India eventually classified sixth.Aichi-Nagoya extended that upward trajectory. India added six medals to its revised Hangzhou total, increased its gold-medal count from 27 to 30 and climbed two places to fourth.The numbers at a glance: India's medal tally increased more than eightfold between 2010 and 2026. Its gold-medal count grew from one to 30, while its position improved from 15th to fourth.The rise has not been limited to the overall tally. India has improved its standing in three successive editions since 2014, moving from 15th to ninth, then sixth and now fourth. The 2026 result represents the culmination of a sustained upward trend rather than an isolated breakthrough.The most striking feature of India's latest performance was the efficiency with which its athletes converted participation into medals.India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi-Nagoya. That was considerably fewer than the 309 athletes listed for the Hangzhou campaign in 2023, yet the team surpassed its previous best by six medals.The comparison is revealing. India sent approximately 46 per cent fewer athletes than it did to Hangzhou, but its medal tally increased by nearly six per cent. The gold-medal count rose by three, the silver tally by three, and the bronze count remained unchanged.On a simple medals-per-athlete measure, India's return increased from approximately 0.35 medals per athlete in Hangzhou to 0.68 in Aichi-Nagoya. This is an aggregate comparison, not an individual success rate, since athletes can win multiple medals and the number of events and opportunities varies across sports.Nevertheless, the figures underline the scale of the achievement. A smaller squad did not merely match the previous edition's success; it established a new benchmark for Indian para-sport.Para-athletics was the backbone of India's campaign, delivering 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. That represented nearly 57 per cent of the country's overall tally and made athletics the single biggest contributor to India's fourth-place finish.Para-badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze. Together, athletics and badminton accounted for 81 medals, more than 70 per cent of India's total.Swimming contributed 11 medals, comprising three silver and eight bronze. Archery added six medals, including three gold and three silver, while shooting produced five, with two gold, two silver and one bronze.Athletics' contribution also illustrates how India's progress has accelerated. At Hangzhou, para-athletics produced 52 medals, including 16 gold, 17 silver and 19 bronze. In Aichi-Nagoya, the discipline's haul rose to 65, with six additional gold medals.Badminton's contribution was different. India won 21 medals in the sport at Hangzhou, including four gold, but finished with 16 in 2026. Instead, the substantial gains in athletics and the contributions from other sports helped compensate for the decline in badminton medals.That distinction matters: the record haul reflects both the strength of India's established medal-winning disciplines and the need to broaden its success across events in future editions.India's record was supported by athletes who delivered more than once during the competition. A total of 26 Indian athletes won multiple medals, while six athletes collected multiple gold medals, demonstrating the importance of individual excellence in a campaign involving 11 sports.Archer Sheetal Devi was among the standout performers, winning two gold medals and a silver. Her two golds came in the mixed compound and individual compound events, while the silver added to her three-medal haul.Athletics provided several other multiple gold medallists. Dilip Gavit, Nishad Kumar, Pranav Soorma and Simran Sharma each won two gold medals, while shooting contributed through Mona Agarwal, who also secured two golds.Four athletes finished with three medals apiece: Sheetal Devi in archery, Thulasimathi Murugesan in badminton, Ravi Budigina in swimming and Himanshu Nandal in swimming. Their performances illustrated how athletes winning across multiple events can make a significant difference to a country's final tally.The figures also invite comparison with Hangzhou, where 25 Indian athletes won multiple medals. The increase to 26 in 2026 was modest, but the overall tally improved despite a much smaller contingent. The result points to a campaign in which medal-winning performances were concentrated among a relatively small squad.India's rise at the Asian Para Games has coincided with a significant improvement at the Paralympics, strengthening the country's standing in international para-sport.At Rio 2016, India won four medals and finished 43rd. Tokyo 2020 marked a breakthrough, with 19 medals — five gold, eight silver and six bronze — lifting India to 24th. At Paris 2024, India recorded its best Paralympic haul of 29 medals, comprising seven gold, nine silver and 13 bronze, to finish 18th.The progression at the Paralympics mirrors the broader trend at the Asian Para Games: larger medal returns, more gold medals and improvements in the standings.India's able-bodied contingent had also finished fourth at the 2026 Asian Games, although its 85-medal tally was below the 106 medals achieved at Hangzhou in 2023. The para contingent's performance offered a contrasting story of growth, with its medal count rising and its position improving.China dominated Aichi-Nagoya, finishing with 435 medals, including 207 gold. Hosts Japan were second with 186 medals, while Uzbekistan finished third with 145. India placed fourth with 114, ahead of South Korea, which collected 100 medals, including 29 gold.India's final position was not guaranteed until the closing stages. South Korea remained within reach, but its final-day return of one gold and two silver left it one gold behind India. The Indian contingent held on to fourth place with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze.The gap to third-placed Uzbekistan shows that further progress will require India to expand its medal-winning strength across disciplines. Yet the immediate achievement is significant: India has moved from 15th at the first two editions to fourth, while increasing its tally at every successive Games.The challenge now is to sustain that momentum, build a deeper pool of competitive athletes and reduce dependence on a handful of disciplines.For a contingent of just 167 athletes, 114 medals represent more than a record. They mark the latest step in a 16-year transformation of Indian para-sport — one that began with 14 medals in Guangzhou and has now culminated in a historic fourth-place finish in Aichi-Nagoya.
Article Summary: India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi- Nagoya. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place. It is the best finish in the country's history at the event.

Article Title: Asian Para Games bronze leaves Suhas Yathiraj hungry for gold amid IAS duties and badminton
Article Text:

Third Paralympics, one big dream: Gold at LA 2028

IAS officer by day, shuttler by night

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Lee Chong Wei 's influence

NEW DELHI: Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. Having beaten Indonesia's Fredy Setiawan in their group match just days earlier, the Indian shuttler had hoped to reach the final and fight for gold.Suhas lost the men's singles SL4 semifinal 23-21, 8-21, 15-21. He had chances to take the opening game but failed to convert them. After bouncing back to win the second game 21-8, he lost focus at a crucial stage of the decider.“Definitely not satisfied with bronze. I think if I had played up to my full potential, I would have definitely done better. In fact, I defeated Fredy of Indonesia in the group match in Nagoya only a few days ago,” Suhas told TimesofIndia.com from Aichi-Nagoya in Japan.“In the semifinal match, the first set was very close. I lost 23-21 and I had game point, set point, but I couldn't convert that. In the second set, I won very easily. In the third set, I think after 10-all, I sort of lost focus for two to three rallies. That is where he took the game. So, it was not my best day, I would assume. I would always love to win a gold medal. So, yes, I am a little sad from that angle,” he said.The defeat also reminded him of how important it is to perform under pressure at major tournaments.“It is the most important factor to win medals at major games because you might be training well, you might actually have the fitness and the skills. But if you don't recreate that during the major games, then probably it is of not much use in terms of professional success,” Suhas said.Suhas, an IAS officer, said he had never imagined representing India in international badminton a decade ago.In November 2016, he made his debut at the Asian Championships in Beijing and won gold. Since then, he has won several medals at major international events. These include bronze at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, silver at the Tokyo 2020 Paralympics, another silver at the Paris 2024 Paralympics, gold at the Hangzhou Asian Para Games and bronze in Nagoya.The 43-year-old has represented India at two Paralympic Games, Tokyo in 2020 and Paris in 2024, winning silver on both occasions.With the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympics approaching, the big question is whether he can go one step further and win gold.The desire is there, but Suhas is not looking too far ahead. He wants to take things one step at a time.“If you had asked me 10 years ago, I didn't even know that I would play for India. But whenever I look at the medals and the love I have got from fans and sportspersons around the world, the journey has been quite satisfying. I have had the honour of wearing the Indian jersey and winning medals for my country,” he said.“I am grateful for what God has given me. I never imagined that I would become an IAS officer one day, an Arjuna awardee or a badminton player winning medals for India. I never imagined all this. But thanks to the Almighty for all these,” Suhas, who is also an Arjuna Award recipient, said.“So if God and destiny have been kind to me, I hope they will take me to a place that I deserve. I hope I can do the best that I can in whatever I choose to,” he added.For most people, the end of a hectic working day is a time to relax, spend time with family, play with their children or watch a movie.For Suhas, it is often time to pick up his badminton racket and head to the court. His day includes early-morning gym sessions, office work, inspections, meetings, video conferences and checking files. Despite his demanding responsibilities as an IAS officer, he makes time for badminton and follows a strict fitness routine to compete at the highest level.Balancing the two careers is not easy, but his love for the sport keeps him going.“If you choose what you love, then the journey becomes painless. You enjoy that journey. That's what I do,” Suhas said.Explaining how he manages his work and training, he said: “It is challenging. My training generally starts in the night and it always involves sacrifices. Probably others would be spending time with their family members or having leisure time. My leisure time is to play badminton. In badminton, you need an extremely high level of fitness. It's challenging, hectic but at the same time I love it.”“I don't remember eating sweets in the last many months. I can't recall when I had my last sweet. So, I almost don't eat sweets or fried food and am also quite conscious about the nutrition that I take,” he said.Suhas grew up watching Malaysian badminton great Lee Chong Wei and was inspired by his movement on the court.“Yes, I have always been inspired by so many top players in the able-bodied category. Growing up, I watched the matches of Lee Chong Wei and how he used to move around the court,” he said.“Even in India, the top shuttlers perform extremely well, whether it is Lakshya Sen, HS Prannoy or Kidambi Srikanth. I know them personally and have always admired how well they are able to compete at the top,” Suhas signed off.
Article Summary: Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. The Indian shuttler lost the men's singles SL4 semifinal 23- 21, 8-21, 15-21. Suhas has represented India at two Paralympic Games, Tokyo in 2020 and Paris in 2024.

NEW DELHI: India signed off from the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games with their best-ever medal haul of 114 medals as the week-long continental competition concluded with a closing ceremony at the Mizuho Park Athletics Stadium in Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday.Double gold medallists Nishad Kumar and Mona Agarwal led the Indian contingent as flag-bearers at the ceremony, marking the end of a landmark campaign in which the country's para-athletes delivered historic victories, world-record performances and podium sweeps across disciplines.India finished fourth in the overall standings with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze medals, surpassing its previous best of 108 medals at the 2022 Hangzhou Games.Held in Japan for the first time, the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games brought together around 4,000 athletes and staff from 45 countries and regions. The competition featured 18 sports, with more than 20 world records reportedly set during the seven-day event.China topped the medal table with 435 medals, including 207 gold, while hosts Japan finished second with 186 medals — 64 gold, 60 silver and 62 bronze.Uzbekistan emerged as the third-ranked nation, collecting 145 medals, including 45 gold.India's fourth-place finish was particularly significant given the size of its contingent. A total of 168 para-athletes represented the country at Aichi-Nagoya, compared with 309 at the previous edition in Hangzhou.President Droupadi Murmu congratulated the Indian contingent on its record performance, saying the achievement reflected the athletes' hard work, perseverance and self-belief.In a post on X, Murmu said the unprecedented medal haul would inspire young people to dream big, work with dedication and remain positive in the face of challenges. She also extended her congratulations to the entire Indian contingent.Para athletics was India's biggest medal contributor, accounting for 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. Asian Paralympic Committee president Majid Rashed declared the event closed, highlighting the growing strength of para sport across Asia and its role in building a more inclusive society.Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also praised the athletes' determination, teamwork and sportsmanship, describing their performances as a reminder of the “profound beauty” of para sports.The Asian Para Games began in Guangzhou, China, in 2010, evolving from the Far East and South Pacific Games Federation for the Disabled. The Aichi-Nagoya edition was the fifth staging of the event, with Doha, Qatar, scheduled to host the sixth in 2030.For India, the closing ceremony marked the end of a historic campaign — one that raised the country's medal benchmark and showcased the depth and growing strength of its para-sport movement.
